title: Lists, Stacks & Queues
scopeHtml: Scope: linked list rewiring, fast/slow pointers, stacks, monotonic stack and deque, LRU cache.

notes.title: Linked list basics and the dummy node
notes.html:
Idea. A linked list stores items in nodes that point to the next node, so insertion and deletion at a known node are O(1) but access by index is O(n). Interview problems are about rewiring pointers carefully, not about the data.

Two habits that prevent most bugs.

  • Use a dummy (sentinel) head so the real head needs no special case when you delete or insert at the front.
  • Save next before you overwrite it.

Worked example: Reverse a linked list (iterative). Walk once, pointing each node back at the previous one.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
struct ListNode { int val; ListNode* next; ListNode(int v) : val(v), next(nullptr) {} };

ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* prev = nullptr;
    while (head) {
        ListNode* nxt = head->next;      // save before overwriting
        head->next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = nxt;
    }
    return prev;
}
class ListNode { int val; ListNode next; ListNode(int v) { val = v; } }

ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;
    while (head != null) {
        ListNode nxt = head.next;        // save before overwriting
        head.next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = nxt;
    }
    return prev;
}
class ListNode(var `val`: Int) { var next: ListNode? = null }

fun reverseList(head: ListNode?): ListNode? {
    var prev: ListNode? = null
    var cur = head
    while (cur != null) {
        val nxt = cur.next               // save before overwriting
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    }
    return prev
}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next                  # save before overwriting
        head.next = prev
        prev, head = head, nxt
    return prev

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space (a recursive version uses O(n) stack).

Language notes for a C++ developer. Java and Kotlin have garbage collection, so there is no delete; Python objects are collected automatically too. In C++ remember to free removed nodes (or use smart pointers). Kotlin needs ListNode? for nullable next, and val is a keyword so it is escaped with backticks.

Industry examples. The Linux kernel and many allocators use linked lists; an LRU cache combines a hash map with a doubly linked list; undo history and browser back stacks are list-like.

Everyday analogy. A scavenger hunt where each clue tells you where the next one is hidden; reversing it means rewriting every clue to point back.

Common interview traps.

  • Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next before saving it.
  • Forgetting to handle the empty list and a single node.
  • Returning head instead of the new head prev.

notes.title: Fast and slow pointers
notes.html:
Idea. Move one pointer one step at a time and another two steps at a time. If there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one; otherwise it reaches the end. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

Worked example: Detect a cycle (Floyd's algorithm).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool hasCycle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode *slow = head, *fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
fun hasCycle(head: ListNode?): Boolean {
    var slow = head
    var fast = head
    while (fast?.next != null) {
        slow = slow!!.next
        fast = fast.next!!.next
        if (slow === fast) return true
    }
    return false
}
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False

Finding where the cycle starts. After they meet, reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle entry.

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space, compared with a hash set of visited nodes at O(n) space.

Other uses. Middle of a list, palindrome linked list (reverse the second half), the n-th node from the end (two pointers n apart), finding a duplicate in an array of 1..n (treat values as next pointers).

Everyday analogy. Two runners on a circular track at different speeds: the faster one must eventually catch the slower one; on a straight road it just finishes.

Common interview traps.

  • Dereferencing fast->next->next without checking fast->next first.
  • Comparing values instead of node identity (== on references or pointers, is in Python).

notes.title: Stack and matching brackets
notes.html:
Idea. A stack is last-in, first-out. It fits "most recent unmatched thing" problems: matching brackets, undo, expression evaluation, DFS without recursion.

Worked example: Valid Parentheses. Push openers; for each closer the top of the stack must be its matching opener.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool isValid(const string& s) {
    stack<char> st;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') st.push(c);
        else {
            if (st.empty()) return false;
            char o = st.top(); st.pop();
            if ((c == ')' && o != '(') || (c == ']' && o != '[') || (c == '}' && o != '{')) return false;
        }
    }
    return st.empty();
}
boolean isValid(String s) {
    Deque<Character> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') st.push(c);
        else {
            if (st.isEmpty()) return false;
            char o = st.pop();
            if ((c == ')' && o != '(') || (c == ']' && o != '[') || (c == '}' && o != '{')) return false;
        }
    }
    return st.isEmpty();
}
fun isValid(s: String): Boolean {
    val pairs = mapOf(')' to '(', ']' to '[', '}' to '{')
    val st = ArrayDeque<Char>()
    for (c in s) {
        if (c in pairs.values) st.addLast(c)
        else if (st.isEmpty() || st.removeLast() != pairs[c]) return false
    }
    return st.isEmpty()
}
def is_valid(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    st = []
    for c in s:
        if c in pairs:
            if not st or st.pop() != pairs[c]:
                return False
        else:
            st.append(c)
    return not st

Complexity. O(n) time, O(n) space.

Language notes. Prefer ArrayDeque over the legacy Stack class in Java; Kotlin's ArrayDeque supports addLast/removeLast; Python lists are stacks with append/pop.

Everyday analogy. A stack of plates: you can only take or add on the top.

Common interview traps.

  • Popping from an empty stack (check first).
  • Forgetting that the stack must be empty at the end (extra openers).

notes.title: Monotonic stack
notes.html:
Idea. Keep a stack whose elements are always sorted (increasing or decreasing). When a new element breaks the order, pop and settle the answer for the popped elements. Each element is pushed and popped once, so it is O(n).

Recognise it when: "next greater element", "days until a warmer temperature", "largest rectangle in a histogram", "stock span".

Worked example: Daily Temperatures. For each day, how many days until a warmer one? Keep a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> dailyTemperatures(vector<int>& t) {
    vector<int> ans(t.size(), 0);
    stack<int> st;                                     // indices, temperatures decreasing
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)t.size(); i++) {
        while (!st.empty() && t[st.top()] < t[i]) {
            ans[st.top()] = i - st.top();
            st.pop();
        }
        st.push(i);
    }
    return ans;
}
int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] t) {
    int[] ans = new int[t.length];
    Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();           // indices, temperatures decreasing
    for (int i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
        while (!st.isEmpty() && t[st.peek()] < t[i]) {
            int j = st.pop();
            ans[j] = i - j;
        }
        st.push(i);
    }
    return ans;
}
fun dailyTemperatures(t: IntArray): IntArray {
    val ans = IntArray(t.size)
    val st = ArrayDeque<Int>()                         // indices, temperatures decreasing
    for (i in t.indices) {
        while (st.isNotEmpty() && t[st.last()] < t[i]) {
            val j = st.removeLast()
            ans[j] = i - j
        }
        st.addLast(i)
    }
    return ans
}
def daily_temperatures(t):
    ans = [0] * len(t)
    st = []                                            # indices, temperatures decreasing
    for i, x in enumerate(t):
        while st and t[st[-1]] < x:
            j = st.pop()
            ans[j] = i - j
        st.append(i)
    return ans

Complexity. O(n) time and space; the inner while pops each index at most once.

Industry examples. Stock "span" indicators, the histogram and maximal rectangle problems used in layout and image analysis, and parsing nested structures.

Everyday analogy. People waiting in a line of increasing height-of-demand: when a taller person arrives, everyone shorter in front is "answered" and leaves the line.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing values instead of indices when you need distances.
  • Wrong comparison direction (< vs <=) for equal elements; decide what "greater" means.
  • Not processing leftover stack elements at the end when the problem requires it (for example the histogram rectangle problem).

notes.title: Queue and the monotonic deque
notes.html:
Idea. A queue is first-in, first-out (BFS, scheduling). A deque supports both ends, and a monotonic deque keeps candidates in sorted order to answer "max/min of every sliding window" in O(n).

Worked example: Sliding Window Maximum. Keep indices in the deque with decreasing values; the front is always the current window's maximum.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> maxSlidingWindow(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    deque<int> dq;                                     // indices, values decreasing
    vector<int> out;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        while (!dq.empty() && dq.front() <= i - k) dq.pop_front();     // out of window
        while (!dq.empty() && a[dq.back()] <= a[i]) dq.pop_back();     // dominated
        dq.push_back(i);
        if (i >= k - 1) out.push_back(a[dq.front()]);
    }
    return out;
}
int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();            // indices, values decreasing
    int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();   // out of window
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) dq.pollLast();   // dominated
        dq.offerLast(i);
        if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
    }
    return out;
}
fun maxSlidingWindow(a: IntArray, k: Int): IntArray {
    val dq = ArrayDeque<Int>()                         // indices, values decreasing
    val out = IntArray(a.size - k + 1)
    for (i in a.indices) {
        while (dq.isNotEmpty() && dq.first() <= i - k) dq.removeFirst()     // out of window
        while (dq.isNotEmpty() && a[dq.last()] <= a[i]) dq.removeLast()     // dominated
        dq.addLast(i)
        if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.first()]
    }
    return out
}
from collections import deque

def max_sliding_window(a, k):
    dq, out = deque(), []                              # indices, values decreasing
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while dq and dq[0] <= i - k:
            dq.popleft()                               # out of window
        while dq and a[dq[-1]] <= x:
            dq.pop()                                   # dominated
        dq.append(i)
        if i >= k - 1:
            out.append(a[dq[0]])
    return out

Complexity. O(n) time, O(k) space, versus O(n·k) for scanning each window or O(n log k) with a heap.

Industry examples. Rolling maxima for monitoring (highest latency in the last minute), queue-based task schedulers, and BFS in graph search.

Everyday analogy. A queue of people where a stronger newcomer makes everyone weaker behind them irrelevant for "who is strongest in the line".

Common interview traps.

  • Storing values instead of indices, so you cannot tell when the front leaves the window.
  • Dropping the <= equality case and keeping stale equal elements.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Linked-list problems are about careful pointer rewiring: use a dummy head, save next before changing it, and handle empty and single-node lists. Fast and slow pointers find cycles and middles in O(1) space. A stack matches nested structure (brackets), and a monotonic stack answers next-greater problems in O(n) by popping while the order breaks. A monotonic deque gives sliding-window maximum in O(n). Always store indices when distances or window bounds matter.

questions.promptHtml: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively. What are the common bugs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The baseline pointer-manipulation problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep prev (initially null) and cur. In each step save next, point cur.next at prev, then advance both. At the end prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space. The common bugs are overwriting next before saving it and returning the old head.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each node's pointer is flipped once. With a recursive solution the stack is O(n). A dummy head helps with deletions and insertions at the front but is not needed for pure reversal.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
struct ListNode { int val; ListNode* next; ListNode(int v) : val(v), next(nullptr) {} };
ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* prev = nullptr;
    while (head) {
        ListNode* nxt = head->next;
        head->next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = nxt;
    }
    return prev;
}
class ListNode { int val; ListNode next; ListNode(int v) { val = v; } }
ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;
    while (head != null) {
        ListNode nxt = head.next;
        head.next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = nxt;
    }
    return prev;
}
class ListNode(var `val`: Int) { var next: ListNode? = null }
fun reverseList(head: ListNode?): ListNode? {
    var prev: ListNode? = null
    var cur = head
    while (cur != null) {
        val nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    }
    return prev
}
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next
        head.next = prev
        prev, head = head, nxt
    return prev

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Losing the remainder of the list by overwriting next.
  • Returning head (now the tail) instead of prev.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Reverse only a sub-range? → Use a dummy head, walk to the node before the range, reverse in place.
  2. Reverse in groups of k? → Reverse each group and reconnect.
  3. Recursive version? → Reverse the rest, then fix head.next.next = head.

sections.html: Senior mentions both versions, stack cost, and in-place sub-range reversal.

questions.promptHtml: Detect a cycle in a linked list in O(1) space and find where it begins.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Floyd's algorithm is a standard and the start-of-cycle step tests deeper understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Move slow one step and fast two steps; if they meet there is a cycle. To find the start, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle entry. O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
If the distance from head to the cycle start is a, and the meeting point is b steps into the cycle, then a equals the remaining cycle length from the meeting point back to the start (modulo the cycle length). That is why walking from the head and from the meeting point at the same speed lands on the entry.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
ListNode* detectCycle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode *slow = head, *fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) {
            slow = head;
            while (slow != fast) { slow = slow->next; fast = fast->next; }
            return slow;
        }
    }
    return nullptr;
}
ListNode detectCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) {
            slow = head;
            while (slow != fast) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next; }
            return slow;
        }
    }
    return null;
}
fun detectCycle(head: ListNode?): ListNode? {
    var slow = head
    var fast = head
    while (fast?.next != null) {
        slow = slow!!.next
        fast = fast.next!!.next
        if (slow === fast) {
            slow = head
            while (slow !== fast) { slow = slow!!.next; fast = fast!!.next }
            return slow
        }
    }
    return null
}
def detect_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            slow = head
            while slow is not fast:
                slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next
            return slow
    return None

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dereferencing fast.next.next without checking fast.next.
  • Comparing values instead of node identity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Length of the cycle? → After meeting, count steps until the pointers meet again.
  2. Middle of a list? → Slow is at the middle when fast reaches the end.
  3. Duplicate number in an array of n+1 values in 1..n? → Same algorithm treating values as next indices.

sections.html: Senior explains the math of why the entry-point trick works.

questions.promptHtml: For each day, find how many days until a warmer temperature. Why is the stack solution O(n)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard monotonic stack problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a stack of indices whose temperatures are decreasing. For each new day, pop every index with a lower temperature and set its answer to the distance. Then push the current index. Each index is pushed and popped once, so it is O(n).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The stack invariant is "days still waiting for a warmer day". A new warmer day resolves all colder days on top of the stack at once. The answer is distance in indices, which is why indices (not values) are stored.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> dailyTemperatures(vector<int>& t) {
    vector<int> ans(t.size(), 0);
    stack<int> st;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)t.size(); i++) {
        while (!st.empty() && t[st.top()] < t[i]) {
            ans[st.top()] = i - st.top();
            st.pop();
        }
        st.push(i);
    }
    return ans;
}
int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] t) {
    int[] ans = new int[t.length];
    Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
        while (!st.isEmpty() && t[st.peek()] < t[i]) {
            int j = st.pop();
            ans[j] = i - j;
        }
        st.push(i);
    }
    return ans;
}
fun dailyTemperatures(t: IntArray): IntArray {
    val ans = IntArray(t.size)
    val st = ArrayDeque<Int>()
    for (i in t.indices) {
        while (st.isNotEmpty() && t[st.last()] < t[i]) {
            val j = st.removeLast()
            ans[j] = i - j
        }
        st.addLast(i)
    }
    return ans
}
def daily_temperatures(t):
    ans = [0] * len(t)
    st = []
    for i, x in enumerate(t):
        while st and t[st[-1]] < x:
            j = st.pop()
            ans[j] = i - j
        st.append(i)
    return ans

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing values, losing the distance.
  • Wrong strictness (< vs <=) for ties.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Largest rectangle in a histogram? → Increasing stack; pop to compute areas, with a sentinel 0 at the end.
  2. Next greater element in a circular array? → Iterate twice over indices modulo n.
  3. Stock span? → Same idea with previous greater.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior proves the amortised bound and handles the histogram variant.

questions.promptHtml: Compute the maximum of every sliding window of size k in O(n).

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the monotonic deque and amortised reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a deque of indices with decreasing values. For each new index drop the front if it left the window, drop from the back while the back's value is not larger than the new value, push the new index, and read the front as the window maximum. O(n) time, O(k) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An element smaller than a later element can never be a maximum while that later element is in the window, so it is discarded. The front always holds the maximum of the current window.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<int> maxSlidingWindow(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    deque<int> dq;
    vector<int> out;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        while (!dq.empty() && dq.front() <= i - k) dq.pop_front();
        while (!dq.empty() && a[dq.back()] <= a[i]) dq.pop_back();
        dq.push_back(i);
        if (i >= k - 1) out.push_back(a[dq.front()]);
    }
    return out;
}
int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
    int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) dq.pollLast();
        dq.offerLast(i);
        if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
    }
    return out;
}
fun maxSlidingWindow(a: IntArray, k: Int): IntArray {
    val dq = ArrayDeque<Int>()
    val out = IntArray(a.size - k + 1)
    for (i in a.indices) {
        while (dq.isNotEmpty() && dq.first() <= i - k) dq.removeFirst()
        while (dq.isNotEmpty() && a[dq.last()] <= a[i]) dq.removeLast()
        dq.addLast(i)
        if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.first()]
    }
    return out
}
from collections import deque

def max_sliding_window(a, k):
    dq, out = deque(), []
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while dq and dq[0] <= i - k:
            dq.popleft()
        while dq and a[dq[-1]] <= x:
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)
        if i >= k - 1:
            out.append(a[dq[0]])
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing values, not indices, so expiry cannot be checked.
  • Using a heap and getting O(n log n) when O(n) is expected.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Minimum per window? → Flip the comparison.
  2. Why not a heap? → O(n log k) with lazy deletion; the deque is simpler and faster.
  3. Shortest subarray with sum ≥ K and negatives? → Deque over prefix sums.

sections.html: Senior compares deque, heap and balanced-tree options.

questions.promptHtml: Check whether a string of brackets is valid. How do you handle multiple bracket types?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A basic stack problem with edge cases.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Push opening brackets; on a closing bracket the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener, otherwise the string is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) time, O(n) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A map from closer to opener keeps the code compact. The stack represents currently open brackets in nesting order, so the most recent opener must be closed first.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool isValid(const string& s) {
    stack<char> st;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') st.push(c);
        else {
            if (st.empty()) return false;
            char o = st.top(); st.pop();
            if ((c == ')' && o != '(') || (c == ']' && o != '[') || (c == '}' && o != '{')) return false;
        }
    }
    return st.empty();
}
boolean isValid(String s) {
    Deque<Character> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') st.push(c);
        else {
            if (st.isEmpty()) return false;
            char o = st.pop();
            if ((c == ')' && o != '(') || (c == ']' && o != '[') || (c == '}' && o != '{')) return false;
        }
    }
    return st.isEmpty();
}
fun isValid(s: String): Boolean {
    val pairs = mapOf(')' to '(', ']' to '[', '}' to '{')
    val st = ArrayDeque<Char>()
    for (c in s) {
        if (c in pairs.values) st.addLast(c)
        else if (st.isEmpty() || st.removeLast() != pairs[c]) return false
    }
    return st.isEmpty()
}
def is_valid(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    st = []
    for c in s:
        if c in pairs:
            if not st or st.pop() != pairs[c]:
                return False
        else:
            st.append(c)
    return not st

1. Minimum insertions to balance? → Track unmatched counts.
  2. Longest valid parentheses? → Stack of indices or DP.
  3. Evaluate an expression with precedence? → Two stacks (shunting-yard).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior extends to expression parsing and compilers.

questions.contextHtml: A service caches the 10,000 most recently used user profiles. The current implementation uses a list scanned linearly for every get and put, and p99 latency has risen to 40 ms under load. You need O(1) get and put with eviction of the least recently used entry.
questions.promptHtml: Design the data structure and explain how it works.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Uses only a hash map (no recency order) or only a list (O(n) search).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single-threaded or concurrent? Fixed capacity? Do reads count as "use"? Time-to-live needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a hash index in front of the list.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Linear scan is the bottleneck; recency tracking is the missing O(1) piece.
  4. How I'd verify: Profile the p99 and count list traversals per request.
  5. Root cause: No direct lookup from key to list position.
  6. Fix: Combine a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. get: look up the node, move it to the front, return the value. put: if present, update and move to front; otherwise insert at the front and if size exceeds capacity remove the tail node and its map entry. Use dummy head and tail nodes to remove edge cases. All operations are O(1).
  7. Prevention: Unit tests for eviction order, capacity 1, and updating an existing key; load test.
  8. Trade-offs: Needs a lock (or sharding by key) under concurrency; Java's LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true) and Python's OrderedDict.move_to_end give this out of the box, but interviewers want the explicit design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Concurrency? → Stripe the cache into shards each with its own lock, or use a concurrent library such as Caffeine.
  • LFU instead? → Frequency buckets with doubly linked lists, still O(1).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Replacing a scanned list with a map plus doubly linked list dropped p99 cache latency from 40 ms to under 1 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: list only or map only.
  • Hire: map plus doubly linked list with O(1) operations.
  • Strong hire: dummy nodes, concurrency, TTL and library alternatives.
